title: Your grief is real, and you are not alone
subtitle: What you are feeling right now is not weakness. It is love, and it belongs here.
body:
When you first learned you were pregnant, something shifted inside you. Even if it was early, even if no one else knew yet—you started to imagine a future. A small face. A tiny hand wrapped around your finger. A lifetime of birthdays and first steps and school uniforms. That future was real to you, and losing it hurts in a way that words cannot fully carry.

You may feel waves of disbelief, as if your mind is still trying to catch up to what has happened. You may feel anger—at your body, at God, at well-meaning people who say the wrong thing. You may feel guilt, turning over everything you ate or did or worried about, searching for a reason. Let me tell you something important: you did not cause this. Miscarriage and stillbirth are almost never caused by something a mother did or did not do. Most early losses happen because the baby was not forming as it should—something completely beyond anyone's control[citation:9].

Grief does not move in a straight line. Some days you will wake up and feel almost normal, and then a song or a smell or a baby on the street will undo you completely. That is not a setback. That is how grief works. It comes in waves, and over time the waves become further apart. They may still be just as tall, but there will be more space between them, and you will learn to breathe again in that space[citation:1].

In many communities in Africa, there is pressure to move on quickly, to try again, to be grateful for what you have. But your grief deserves space. It is not disrespectful to your living children to mourn the one you lost. It is not a lack of faith to feel shattered. Even in cultures where motherhood is seen as a woman's highest calling, where a woman without a living child may feel invisible or incomplete, your worth was never measured only by the children you carry[citation:4]. You are a whole person, and your pain matters.

If you have no one to talk to who understands, consider writing a letter to your baby. Tell them what you dreamed for them. Tell them how much you wanted them to stay. That letter is not for anyone else—it is for you, a way to hold the love that still lives inside you[citation:5]. And when you are ready, find someone who will simply sit with you without trying to fix anything. Someone who will let you cry, or be silent, or speak your baby's name. That alone can be a kind of medicine.
keyTakeaway: Your grief is not something to get over. It is something to move through, one breath at a time, and you do not have to do it alone.

title: When the world expects you to be "fine"
subtitle: Other people may not understand. That does not mean your pain is wrong.
body:
One of the hardest parts of pregnancy loss is that the world often does not know how to hold your grief. If your loss was early, people may say things like, 'At least it happened early,' or 'You can try again.' If your loss was later, people may avoid you altogether, unsure of what to say, afraid of making things worse. Some may even act as if nothing happened, because acknowledging your baby feels too uncomfortable for them.

This is called disenfranchised grief—grief that society does not fully recognize or validate[citation:9]. When a grandmother dies, there is a funeral, a burial, a clear space for mourning. When a marriage ends, people understand there is a period of sadness. But when you lose a pregnancy, many people expect you to simply try again, as if the baby you lost was only a possibility, not a real person. But you know differently. You held that hope. You loved that child. That love does not disappear just because they never took a breath outside your body.

You may find yourself feeling angry or jealous when you see pregnant women or new babies. You may want to hide from baby showers or skip family gatherings where children will be present. These feelings are not ugly or shameful. They are the natural response of a heart that is still healing. Give yourself permission to step away from situations that feel too heavy right now[citation:9]. You do not have to explain yourself to anyone. A simple 'I am not feeling up to it today' is enough.

If you are struggling with what to say to people who hurt you with their words, remember that you do not have to educate everyone. For those closest to you, you might say, 'What I need right now is for you to just listen. I do not need solutions or silver linings. I just need you to be here.' For those who cannot give you that, it is okay to create distance. Protect your heart like you would protect a healing wound. Let it rest.

Over time, you may find that your grief becomes more private, something you carry rather than something that carries you. You may learn which friends and family members can hold space for you and which ones cannot. And you may discover a strength in yourself that you did not know was there—the strength to keep going, even when going is hard.
keyTakeaway: You do not owe anyone a performance of being "over it." Grieve at your own pace, and protect your heart from people who cannot honour your pain.

title: What your body needs right now
subtitle: After loss or delivery, your body is doing quiet, important work. Here is how to support it.
body:
Your body has been through something profound. Whether you delivered a baby who could not stay, or you are recovering from a miscarriage or a procedure, your physical self needs care and patience. You may be bleeding, cramping, feeling tired in a way that sleep does not fix. Your hormones are shifting rapidly, and that alone can make you feel unlike yourself—tearful, irritable, exhausted, or numb.

In the first days and weeks after loss, rest is not a luxury. It is medicine. Your uterus is shrinking back to its usual size, and your body is using energy to heal. If you had a D&C or a delivery, there is also the healing of your cervix and possibly stitches. This is not the time to prove how strong you are by returning to all your normal duties. If you can, let others cook, clean, and care for other children. If you cannot, lower your expectations for yourself. A day when you eat, drink water, and rest is a successful day.

Watch for signs that your body needs more help. Heavy bleeding—soaking a pad in less than an hour—is not normal. Fever, chills, severe pain, or discharge that smells bad could mean an infection. Do not ignore these signs or tell yourself you are being dramatic. Your health matters. If something feels wrong, go to a clinic or hospital. It is always better to be seen and told you are fine than to wait and risk complications.

For most women, bleeding after a miscarriage or delivery lasts about one to two weeks, though it can come and go. Your next period may return in four to six weeks, but it can take longer, especially if your body is under stress. Do not be alarmed if your first few cycles are irregular or different from before—heavier, lighter, more painful. This is common. Give your body time to find its rhythm again.

Restoring your physical strength also means eating, even when you have no appetite. Small, simple meals are enough: porridge, broth with vegetables, eggs, beans, rice. Your body needs iron especially, because you have lost blood. Dark greens, beans, and small amounts of red meat or chicken liver can help. Drink water, even if you do not feel thirsty. Dehydration will only make the fatigue worse.

Above all, be gentle with yourself. Your body did not fail you. It carried life, even if that life was shorter than you dreamed. Treat it with the same tenderness you would offer a friend who had just survived something hard. You deserve that kindness.
keyTakeaway: Rest, eat small nourishing meals, watch for warning signs, and give your body time to heal without rushing.

title: Healing after delivery — your body, your timeline
subtitle: Whether you gave birth yesterday or six months ago, your body is still adjusting. That is completely normal.
body:
Bringing a baby into the world is one of the most demanding things a human body can do. Even when everything goes smoothly, your body needs time to recover. If you had a vaginal delivery, your perineum may be sore or swollen. If you had a C‑section, you have a wound that reaches through several layers of tissue, and healing takes longer than you might expect—often six weeks or more before you feel like yourself again.

Bleeding after delivery, called lochia, can last four to six weeks. It will change from bright red to pink to brown to yellow-white. This is normal. What is not normal is bleeding that suddenly becomes heavy again after it had slowed, passing clots larger than your thumb, or developing a fever. These can be signs of infection or retained placental tissue, and you should see a nurse or doctor.

Many new mothers feel pressure to recover quickly, to return to housework, to care for everyone else. But your body is doing invisible work: your uterus is shrinking, your abdominal muscles are slowly knitting back together, your hormones are rebalancing. This work takes energy. If you feel exhausted, it is because you are. Give yourself permission to rest, to nap when the baby naps, to ask for help with lifting and carrying.

Pay attention to your scar if you had a C‑section. Keep it clean and dry. Redness, swelling, oozing, or increasing pain are signs of infection. Do not lift anything heavier than your baby for the first six weeks. Pushing too hard too soon can delay healing or cause complications. Walking is good; running or heavy lifting is not.

Your emotions are also part of your physical recovery. The drop in oestrogen and progesterone after birth can trigger mood swings, tearfulness, and anxiety—sometimes called the baby blues. These usually last a week or two. If the sadness does not lift, or if you feel hopeless, panicky, or unable to bond with your baby, you may have postpartum depression. That is not a weakness. It is a medical condition, and it can be treated. Speak to a health worker you trust.

Your body grew a human. It may look different now—softer in some places, marked with lines, carrying a scar. That is not damage. That is evidence of what you have done. Be proud of it, and be patient with it. You are healing, and healing takes the time it takes.
keyTakeaway: Postpartum recovery takes weeks, not days. Listen to your body, watch for warning signs, and ask for help when you need it.

title: When sadness stays longer than expected
subtitle: How to recognise depression after loss and what you can do about it
body:
Sadness after losing a pregnancy is not only normal—it is expected. But sometimes sadness hardens into something heavier. Something that does not lift, even on days when you want it to. Depression after pregnancy loss is real, and it is more common than people talk about.

You may be experiencing depression if you have been feeling hopeless for weeks, not just hours or days. If nothing brings you pleasure anymore—not food, not time with loved ones, not activities you used to enjoy. If you are sleeping too much or too little, eating too much or nothing at all. If you feel worthless, or guilty even when you have done nothing wrong. If you have thoughts that you would be better off dead, or that your family would be better without you.

These thoughts are not your fault. They are symptoms, like a fever or a cough. They do not mean you are weak or broken. They mean your brain is struggling, and it needs help—just as your body would need help if you had a deep wound that would not close.

One of the cruelest parts of depression is that it convinces you that reaching out is pointless. That no one will understand. That you are burdening others. But the opposite is true. Reaching out is the most important thing you can do. Talk to a nurse, a counsellor, a trusted friend, or a support group. In many parts of Africa, mental health services are limited, but there are still options: some clinics have trained counsellors, there are helplines, and increasingly, there are peer support groups for women who have experienced loss[citation:6]. Even speaking to a priest or imam who is gentle and non-judgmental can be a first step.

If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please tell someone immediately. Go to a clinic. Call a helpline. Tell a neighbour. You do not have to carry this alone. Suicide crisis lines in Kenya include 1199 (free) and 0800-723-253. In South Africa, call SADAG at 0800 567 567. These numbers exist because people like you matter, and there is help available.

Recovery from depression is possible. It may take medication, counselling, or both. It will definitely take time. But with support, the heaviness can lift. You can feel joy again. You can find meaning again. The love you felt for your baby does not have to become a weight that drowns you. It can become something you carry with more ease, one day at a time.

Be as kind to yourself as you would be to a sister or a friend who was suffering. You would not tell her to just snap out of it. You would sit with her, bring her tea, and help her find someone who knows how to help. Do that for yourself too.
keyTakeaway: Depression after loss is a real medical condition, not a weakness. Help is available, and you deserve to receive it.

title: Anxiety and the "what if" thoughts
subtitle: How to manage the racing mind that keeps you stuck in fear
body:
After a loss, your mind may become a place of constant alarm. Every twinge in your body becomes a warning. Every quiet moment fills with images of what happened. You may find yourself unable to sleep, or you may wake in the night with your heart pounding, convinced something terrible is about to happen.

This is anxiety, and it is a common companion to grief. Your brain has learned that danger is real, that the worst can happen, and it is trying to protect you by staying alert all the time. But living in a state of high alert is exhausting, and it keeps you from healing.

Anxiety shows up in many ways: racing thoughts that you cannot stop, a constant sense of dread, physical symptoms like a fast heartbeat, shortness of breath, or tightness in your chest. You may avoid places, people, or situations that remind you of your loss. You may find yourself checking and rechecking things, as if control could keep bad things away.

One of the most helpful things you can do for anxiety is to ground yourself in the present moment. When the fear spirals, try this: Look around and name five things you can see. Four things you can touch. Three things you can hear. Two things you can smell. One thing you can taste. This exercise pulls your brain out of the future (where danger lives) and into the now (where you are safe, at least in this moment).

Another helpful practice is to give your worry a container. Set aside ten minutes each day—at the same time, if possible—to sit with your fears. Write them down. Let yourself feel them. When the time is up, close the notebook and tell yourself, 'I will come back to this tomorrow.' This trains your brain that worry has a time and a place, and it does not need to take over your whole day.

If your anxiety is affecting your ability to eat, sleep, or care for yourself, please speak to a health worker. There are treatments that work, including counselling and sometimes medication. You do not have to live in a state of constant fear. With support, you can learn to quiet the alarm and find peace again.
keyTakeaway: Anxiety after loss is your brain trying to protect you, but you can learn to calm it with grounding techniques and professional support.

title: Grieving together, even when you grieve differently
subtitle: How to stay connected with your partner when loss has pulled you apart
body:
Losing a baby can place immense strain on even the strongest relationship. You and your partner may grieve in completely different ways. One of you may need to talk about the baby constantly, to say their name, to hold something that belonged to them. The other may need silence, distraction, time alone. Neither way is wrong. But when your needs clash, it can feel like you are grieving alone, even though you are in the same house.

Men and women often process loss differently, and this is not because one loves more or less. Hormones play a role in how deeply and physically a mother feels the loss[citation:1]. A father may feel he needs to be strong for you, so he hides his own tears. Or he may throw himself into work, unable to sit still with the pain. This can leave you feeling abandoned, as if he has already moved on. He has not. He is just trying to survive in his own way.

One of the most destructive forces in a relationship after loss is blame. You may blame yourself, and you may find yourself blaming him. 'If only you had been there.' 'If only you had not made me stressed.' These thoughts are poisonous, and they are almost never true. Most pregnancy losses cannot be prevented by anything you or your partner did or did not do. Blame will not bring your baby back. It will only drive the two of you further apart[citation:1].

Instead, try to talk about what you need without assuming the other person should know. Say, 'I need you to hold me right now, even if I cry.' Or, 'I need to be alone for an hour, and it is not because I am angry at you.' Ask the same of your partner: 'What do you need from me today?' Sometimes the answer will be, 'I do not know.' That is okay too.

If you can, find a way to honour your baby together. Light a candle. Plant a tree. Write a letter to your baby and read it to each other. Create a small ritual that belongs to the two of you. This will not erase the pain, but it can remind you that you are a team, facing the same loss, even if you face it differently.

If you are struggling to communicate, consider seeing a counsellor together for a few sessions. This is not a sign that your marriage is broken. It is a sign that you care enough to repair it. Many couples find that working through the grief together, with guidance, actually strengthens their bond in the long run.
keyTakeaway: You and your partner may grieve differently. Do not let blame or silence create distance. Talk about what you need, and honour your baby together.

title: What to say to family and friends (and what not to accept)
subtitle: How to set boundaries with well-meaning people who say the wrong thing
body:
People want to help, but they often do not know how. In many communities, there is a deep discomfort around death, especially the death of a baby. People may say things like, 'God needed another angel,' or 'At least you already have other children,' or 'You are young, you can try again.' They mean well. But their words can feel like salt in an open wound.

It is okay to be hurt by what people say. It is okay to feel angry. Your baby was not a lesson or a test. Your other children do not replace the one you lost. And 'trying again' is not the same as having this baby, the one you already love.

You do not have to accept every comment with grace. You are allowed to set boundaries. For close family and friends, you might say, 'I know you mean well, but when you say that, it makes me feel like my baby did not matter. What I really need is for you to just listen.' For acquaintances or people you see less often, a simple 'I am not ready to talk about it' is enough.

If you are the one trying to support a friend who has lost a baby, the best thing you can offer is presence, not advice. Do not try to explain why it happened. Do not offer platitudes. Just be there. Say, 'I am so sorry. I am here.' Ask, 'How are you today?' not 'How are you?' The word 'today' makes space for the fact that grief changes from day to day[citation:1]. Bring food. Do laundry. Watch her other children for an hour. Show up without being asked.

If you feel that your community is not supporting you in the way you need, look for support groups, either in person or online. There are women all over the world who have walked this road, and many of them are waiting to hold space for you. You do not have to educate your entire village. You just need one or two people who truly see you.
keyTakeaway: You have the right to set boundaries with people who hurt you, even unintentionally. Find the few who truly listen, and lean on them.

title: Eating to heal, even when you have no appetite
subtitle: Simple, nourishing foods that support your body after loss or delivery
body:
After a loss or delivery, food may be the last thing on your mind. You may feel too tired to cook, too sad to eat, or too overwhelmed to think about nutrition. But your body is working hard to heal, and it needs fuel. The good news is that eating to recover does not require complicated meals or expensive ingredients. Simple, whole foods can give your body what it needs.

Iron is especially important after you have lost blood. Low iron leaves you feeling weak, dizzy, and more exhausted than you already are. Good sources of iron include dark green leafy vegetables like spinach, amaranth (terere/mchicha), and pumpkin leaves. Beans, lentils, and peas are also excellent, and they are affordable in most markets. If you eat meat, small amounts of beef, goat, chicken liver, or fish can boost your iron quickly. Eating vitamin C at the same time—a tomato, an orange, some fresh papaya—helps your body absorb the iron better.

Protein helps repair tissue, whether you had a miscarriage, a D&C, or a delivery. Eggs are a wonderful source, as are beans, groundnuts, simsim (sesame), and fish. If you can afford milk or yogurt, those help too. Aim to include some protein in every meal, even if it is just a spoonful of peanut butter on bread.

Water is medicine. Bleeding, breastfeeding, and the general stress of grief all dehydrate you. Dehydration makes fatigue worse and can cause headaches and dizziness. Keep a cup of water beside you and sip throughout the day. Soups and broths count too. If plain water is hard to drink, try adding a squeeze of lemon or a piece of ginger.

If you have no appetite, do not force yourself to eat large meals. Instead, eat small amounts often—a handful of groundnuts, a banana, a boiled egg, a piece of chapati with soup. These small meals are easier to tolerate and still give your body energy.

Avoid too much sugar and very fatty foods. They may feel comforting in the moment, but they can leave you feeling more tired afterward. Give yourself grace, though. If all you can eat today is tea and bread, that is still something. Tomorrow, try for a little more. Healing is not about perfection. It is about showing up, one small meal at a time.
keyTakeaway: Focus on iron-rich foods, protein, and water. Eat small meals if large ones feel impossible. Your body needs fuel to heal.

title: Deciding if and when to try again
subtitle: How to know if you are emotionally and physically ready for another pregnancy
body:
After a loss, the question of another pregnancy can feel both urgent and terrifying. You may desperately want to be pregnant again, as if a new pregnancy could fill the emptiness left by the one you lost. Or you may feel that you could never survive another loss, that the fear is too great, that your body cannot be trusted. Both feelings are normal. Both are part of the complicated dance of grief and hope.

There is no right amount of time to wait before trying again. Your body will have its own timeline. Most doctors recommend waiting at least one to three months after a miscarriage, and longer after a stillbirth or C-section, to allow your uterus to heal and your nutrient stores to replenish. But emotional readiness is just as important as physical readiness. You can be physically healed and still not be ready in your heart.

Ask yourself these questions, not to judge your answers, but to understand where you are: Do I feel that I have grieved this loss, or am I trying to replace this baby with another? Can I imagine handling the anxiety of a future pregnancy—the waiting, the uncertainty, the fear of loss again? Do I have support—a partner, a friend, a counsellor—who will walk with me through the fear? Am I sleeping and eating reasonably well, or am I still in a place of deep depletion?

If your answer to many of these is 'no,' that is not failure. It just means you need more time. Pushing yourself into a pregnancy before you are ready can make the anxiety much worse. Many women who try again too soon find that they cannot enjoy the pregnancy at all, only white-knuckle through it, terrified at every appointment[citation:7].

On the other hand, some women find that trying again is part of their healing. It gives them a focus, a reason to hope, a way to look forward rather than only back. That is valid too. The key is honesty with yourself and with your partner about where you stand.

When you do decide to try again, talk to a healthcare provider first. Ask them what, if anything, might be different this time. Will they monitor you more closely? Are there supplements or medications that could help? For some women with a history of preterm loss, progesterone injections or a cervical stitch can make a difference[citation:7]. For many, there is nothing specific to do except to try again with the knowledge that most women who experience a loss go on to have a healthy pregnancy.

And if you try and it takes time, do not let the waiting destroy you. Each month that your period arrives can feel like another loss. Be gentle with yourself. You are not broken. Your body is not a machine. It is a living thing, and like all living things, it moves at its own pace.
keyTakeaway: There is no fixed timeline for trying again. Wait until both your body and your heart feel ready, and talk to a healthcare provider first.

title: Prenatal care when you are already anxious
subtitle: How to protect your peace while protecting your baby's health
body:
Being pregnant after a loss is different. The joy is there, but it often sits alongside fear. You may find yourself holding your breath between appointments, bracing for bad news. Every twinge, every change in your body, every day without feeling the baby move can send you into a spiral of worry. This is not a weakness. It is the natural response of a heart that has already been broken.

Prenatal care is essential, but it can also be a source of anxiety. Walking into a clinic may bring back memories of the day you learned your baby had died. Seeing other pregnant women, hearing babies cry, sitting in the same waiting room—all of this can trigger intense emotion. If you can, bring someone with you to appointments—a partner, a friend, your mother. Someone who can hold your hand, take notes, and remember what the nurse said, because you may be too anxious to absorb it.

Be honest with your healthcare provider about your history. Tell them, 'I had a loss before, and I am very anxious about this pregnancy. Can you explain things to me clearly? Can you tell me what is normal and what I should worry about?' A good provider will understand and will adjust their communication to help you feel safer. They may offer more frequent check-ins, additional ultrasounds, or simply a few extra minutes to answer your questions.

During pregnancy after loss, many women find it helpful to focus on what they can control. You cannot control whether this pregnancy will end well. But you can attend your appointments, take your prenatal vitamins, eat nourishing food, rest when you can, and avoid alcohol and smoking. These small acts of care are not guarantees, but they are expressions of love for the baby you are carrying and for yourself.

It is also important to plan for the hard days. Identify ahead of time what helps you when the anxiety spikes. Maybe it is calling your partner. Maybe it is walking outside. Maybe it is a breathing exercise: breathe in for four counts, hold for four, breathe out for six. Find something that works for you and keep it ready.

If the anxiety becomes overwhelming—if you cannot eat, cannot sleep, cannot function—please speak to a mental health professional. There are counsellors who specialise in pregnancy after loss. They can give you tools to manage the fear, so that the pregnancy is not just something to survive, but something you can eventually find joy in.
keyTakeaway: Pregnancy after loss is hard, but you can do it. Be honest with your provider, bring support to appointments, and have a plan for anxious moments.

title: The fourth trimester — what no one told you
subtitle: Your body, your emotions, and your new life with a newborn
body:
You have done it. You have brought your baby home, or you are preparing to. The pregnancy is over, the delivery is behind you, and now you are in a new season—sometimes called the fourth trimester. This is the first three months after birth, when your body is healing, your hormones are settling, and you are learning who this new person is and who you are as their mother.

No one warns you how hard this can be. The sleep deprivation is real, and it makes everything feel heavier. Your body may still ache. If you are breastfeeding, you may be dealing with sore nipples, engorgement, or worries about whether your baby is getting enough. You may feel overwhelmed, tearful, or strangely disconnected from the baby you waited so long for. This does not mean you are a bad mother. It means you are human.

One of the most important things you can do in the fourth trimester is lower your expectations. Not of your baby—of yourself. Your house does not need to be clean. You do not need to cook elaborate meals. You do not need to entertain visitors or return every message. Your only jobs right now are to rest when you can, feed your baby, and let your body heal. Everything else can wait.

If you are breastfeeding, remember that fed is best. If breastfeeding is working for you and your baby, that is wonderful. But if it is causing you extreme pain, or if your baby is not gaining weight, or if you are simply exhausted and overwhelmed, formula is not failure. The most important thing for your baby is a mother who is not drowning in stress. A calm, supported mother who uses formula is better than a broken mother who forces herself to breastfeed. The research shows that supporting a mother's feeding choices—whatever they are—is what protects against postpartum depression, not the breastmilk itself[citation:2][citation:6].

Watch for signs of postpartum depression. The baby blues—tearfulness, mood swings, anxiety—usually last a week or two. If the sadness does not lift, or if you feel hopeless, unable to bond with your baby, or have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, please get help immediately. Postpartum depression is not your fault, and it can be treated.

Finally, do not try to do this alone. Accept help when it is offered. Let someone else hold the baby while you shower. Let a neighbour bring a meal. Let your mother or sister stay for a few days if that is helpful. You are not supposed to be superhuman. You are supposed to be a mother, which is already more than enough.
keyTakeaway: The first three months after birth are intense. Rest, accept help, feed your baby however works for you, and watch for signs of postpartum depression.

title: Eating well when money is tight and time is shorter
subtitle: Affordable, nutrient-rich foods that support you and your baby
body:
Good nutrition does not require expensive supplements or imported foods. Across Africa, traditional foods are often the most nourishing options available. The challenge is knowing which foods give you the most value for your money, especially when you are feeding a growing baby inside you or recovering from birth while caring for a newborn.

If you are pregnant or trying to regain strength after loss or delivery, focus on three things: iron, protein, and folate. Iron builds your blood and prevents the exhaustion of anaemia. The best affordable sources are dark green leafy vegetables like cassava leaves, pumpkin leaves, amaranth (terere), and blackjack (bidens pilosa). These grow in many home gardens or can be bought cheaply at local markets. Cooking them with a little oil or alongside a small piece of meat or fish helps your body absorb the iron.

Protein does not have to come from expensive meat. Eggs are an excellent source, and many women have access to chickens. Beans, lentils, cowpeas, and groundnuts are also protein-rich and can be stored for a long time. If you eat fish, small dried fish like omena (dagaa) are affordable and packed with calcium and iron. A small handful added to stew or sukuma wiki goes a long way.

Folate is especially important in early pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects, but it matters for recovery too. Dark leafy greens are again your best friend. Pumpkin, sweet potato leaves, and broccoli if available. Orange fruits like pawpaw and oranges also provide vitamin C, which helps your body use the iron you eat.

Eating regularly is more important than eating large amounts. If you feel nauseous or have no appetite, try eating five or six small meals a day instead of three big ones. A handful of groundnuts, a piece of fruit, a boiled egg, a cup of porridge—these are all meals. Do not skip breakfast. Even a small bowl of millet or sorghum porridge gives you energy for the day.

Drink water. In many communities, women are told to avoid cold water or to drink less fluid during pregnancy. This is not correct. Your body needs water to build blood, produce amniotic fluid, and keep you from getting constipated or developing a urinary infection. Aim for six to eight cups a day. If clean water is hard to access, boil it if you can, or use water from a trusted source.

Finally, listen to your body. Cravings are not always random—they may be your body asking for a nutrient it needs. If you crave red meat, you may need iron. If you crave sour things like tamarind or lemon, you may need vitamin C. If you crave ice or clay (pica), that can be a sign of severe iron deficiency, and you should see a nurse. Give yourself permission to eat what your body asks for, within reason. You are not being greedy. You are growing a human, or healing from having done so.
keyTakeaway: You do not need expensive food to eat well. Dark leafy greens, eggs, beans, groundnuts, and small fish give you the iron, protein, and vitamins you need.
